questions.stem: Let A and B be non-empty subsets of a universal set U, then which of the following is false?
explanation_steps: A: (A ∩ B) ∪ A′ = (A ∪ A′) ∩ (B ∪ A′) = U ∩ (B ∪ A′) = B ∪ A′, which is not B in general (e.g. U = {1, 2, 3}, A = {1}, B = {1, 2}: B ∪ A′ = {1, 2, 3} ≠ B). FALSE.
B: A ∩ B ⊆ A, and nothing is in both A and A′, so the result is ∅. True.
C: A ∪ A′ = U already, so (A ∪ B′) ∪ A′ = U. True.
D: (A ∪ B) ∩ B′ = (A ∩ B′) ∪ (B ∩ B′) = A ∩ B′ = A − B. True.
E: (A ∩ B′) ∪ B = (A ∪ B) ∩ (B′ ∪ B) = A ∪ B. True. Answer: A.
tips: Test identities with a small example (Venn diagram or U = {1, 2, 3, 4}); one counter-example proves a statement false.
A − B = A ∩ B′.

similar_questions.stem: For subsets A and B of U, which statement is always true?
explanation_steps: A ∩ (A ∪ B) = A (absorption law): every element of A is in A ∪ B.
A − B ≠ B − A in general; De Morgan gives (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′; A ∪ A′ = U; (A − B) ∩ A = A − B. Answer: C.

questions.stem: If a and b are two real numbers such that |a + b| = |a| + |b|, then which of the following is false?
explanation_steps: |a + b| = |a| + |b| holds exactly when a and b do not have opposite signs, i.e. when ab ≥ 0.
A (both ≥ 0), B (both ≤ 0) and C (a = b gives ab = a² ≥ 0) are all consistent with the equation.
D: a > 0 and b < 0 gives ab < 0, e.g. a = 2, b = −1: |1| = 1 but |2| + |−1| = 3. So D cannot happen – it is the false statement. Answer: D.
tips: Triangle inequality: |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|, with equality only when a and b have the same sign (or one is 0).

similar_questions.stem: For which pair of numbers is |a + b| < |a| + |b|?
explanation_steps: |a + b| < |a| + |b| exactly when a and b have opposite signs.

explanation_steps: C: for x = 2m the line gives y = 4m = 2(2m) = 2n ✓.
A needs n² = 2m² (but n² = 4m²); B needs 2n² = 2m²; D needs 4n = 4m; E needs 2n = 8m – all fail unless m = 0. Answer: C.
tips: Points on a line through the origin stay on it when both coordinates are multiplied by the same number.

questions.stem: If the system of equations { kx + 2y = 4 ; 2x − 4y = −8 } has infinitely many solutions, then the possible value of k is
explanation_steps: Infinitely many solutions ⇔ the two equations are multiples of each other: k/2 = 2/(−4) = 4/(−8).

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about the graph of y = ax² + c, where a and c are real numbers and a ≠ 0?

options.A: If c > 0, then the graph opens upward.
options.B: The vertex of the graph is the point (a, c).
options.C: If a > 0, then the range is all real numbers greater than or equal to c.
options.D: If c > 0, then the range is greater than 0.

explanation_steps: The vertex of y = ax² + c is (0, c) (B false).
The direction of opening depends on a, not c (A false).
If a > 0 the parabola opens upward and its lowest point is (0, c), so the range is {y : y ≥ c} – C is true.
D fails when a < 0 (e.g. y = −x² + 1 takes negative values). Answer: C.
tips: a > 0 → opens up, minimum = c; a < 0 → opens down, maximum = c.

similar_questions.stem: For y = −2x² + 5, which is true?
explanation_steps: a = −2 < 0: opens downward, vertex (0, 5) is the highest point.

The total number of games played by all the teams in a single round play is $\dfrac{t^{2}-t}{2}$. Then how many teams are present in the city if the total games played in a single round is 36?
explanation_steps: t = 9 (t = −8 is impossible for a number of teams). Check: (81 − 9)/2 = 36 ✓. Answer: D.
tips: Reject negative roots in real-life problems.
You can also test the options: 9 × 8 ÷ 2 = 36.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about any polynomial of degree 4?

options.A: It has at most four roots.
options.C: Its domain is all real numbers.
options.D: Its range cannot be all real numbers.

explanation_steps: A: a polynomial of degree n has at most n real roots – true.
B: false – e.g. x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = (x² − 1)(x² − 4) has four x-intercepts (±1, ±2) and x⁴ + 1 has none.
C: every polynomial is defined for all real x – true.
D: an even-degree polynomial has either a minimum or a maximum value, so its range is never all of ℝ – true.
E: x⁴ + 1 = 0 has no real root – true. Answer: B.
tips: Even degree → both ends go the same way → range bounded on one side.
Odd degree → at least one real root.

similar_questions.stem: Which statement is true for every polynomial of degree 3?

options.A: It has exactly three real roots
options.B: It has at least one real root

explanation_steps: An odd-degree polynomial goes to −∞ at one end and +∞ at the other, so it crosses the x-axis at least once.
It may have 1, 2 or 3 distinct real roots. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Given the data 6, 5, 4, 7, 6, 5, 6, 10, 4, then which of the following is true?

options.A: The mode is greater than the median.
options.B: The mean is equal to the mode.
options.C: The mean is less than the median.
options.D: The mode is less than the median.

explanation_steps: Median = 5th value = 6. Mode = 6 (appears three times). Mean = 53 ÷ 9 ≈ 5.89.
Mean (5.89) < median (6) – C is true; mode = median so A and D are false; mean ≠ mode so B is false. Answer: C.
tips: Always order the data before finding the median.

similar_questions.stem: For the data 3, 8, 5, 3, 6, which is true?
explanation_steps: mean = median = 5, mode = 3 is smaller than both. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Given the data 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 7. If 2 is added to each of the numbers, then which of the following is true?

options.A: The new mean is 2 times the original mean.
options.C: The new range is greater than the original range.
options.D: The new standard deviation is 2 times the original standard deviation.

explanation_steps: Adding a constant shifts every value and the mean by 2, so each deviation (xᵢ − x̄) is unchanged.
Hence the variance σ² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/N and the standard deviation stay the same, and the range stays 7 − 0 = 7.
Original mean = 21/7 = 3, new mean = 5 (not 2 × 3). Answer: B.
tips: Adding c: mean + c, spread unchanged. Multiplying by c: mean × c, SD × |c|, variance × c².

questions.stem: Which of the following is a one to one function?
explanation_steps: A function is one-to-one if different inputs always give different outputs (horizontal line test).
|x + 1| gives the same value for x = 0 and x = −2; y = 8.5 and y = |9| are constant; x² − 4x gives 0 at x = 0 and x = 4.
y = 2x − 4 is a non-horizontal line: 2x₁ − 4 = 2x₂ − 4 ⇒ x₁ = x₂. Answer: D.
tips: Every non-constant linear function is one-to-one; quadratics, absolute-value and constant functions are not (on ℝ).

similar_questions.stem: Which function is one-to-one on the set of real numbers?
explanation_steps: x³ + 1 is strictly increasing, so it passes the horizontal line test.
The others take some value twice. Answer: B.

questions.stem: If 8 and 2 are the roots (solutions) of x² + bx + c = 0 and 3 is the only root of x² + dx + e = 0, where b, c, d and e are real numbers, then the roots of x² + bx + e = 0 are
explanation_steps: Roots 8 and 2: x² + bx + c = (x − 8)(x − 2) = x² − 10x + 16, so b = −10.
Only root 3 (double root): x² + dx + e = (x − 3)² = x² − 6x + 9, so e = 9.
x² + bx + e = x² − 10x + 9 = (x − 1)(x − 9) = 0 ⇒ x = 1 or 9. Answer: A.
tips: Sum of roots = −b, product = c (for x² + bx + c).
'Only one root' means a repeated root: discriminant = 0.

questions.stem: The solution set of log₃(x − 1) < log₂(x − 1) is
explanation_steps: Domain: x − 1 > 0 ⇒ x > 1. Let t = x − 1 > 0.
Change of base: log₃t = ln t/ln 3 and log₂t = ln t/ln 2, with ln 3 > ln 2 > 0.
So log₃t < log₂t ⇔ ln t·(1/ln 3 − 1/ln 2) < 0 ⇔ ln t > 0 (because 1/ln 3 − 1/ln 2 < 0) ⇔ t > 1.
x − 1 > 1 ⇒ x > 2. (For 1 < x < 2 the inequality is reversed; at x = 2 both sides are 0.) Answer: A.
tips: Quick check with numbers: x = 9 → log₃8 ≈ 1.89 < log₂8 = 3 ✓; x = 1.5 → log₃0.5 ≈ −0.63 > log₂0.5 = −1 ✗.
For t > 1, the smaller base gives the larger logarithm.

similar_questions.stem: The solution set of log₂(x + 3) > log₄(x + 3) is
explanation_steps: Let t = x + 3 > 0. log₄t = ½ log₂t, so the inequality is log₂t > ½ log₂t ⇔ log₂t > 0 ⇔ t > 1.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about the rational function defined by f(x) = (x − 2)/(x² − 2x − 3)?
questions.stem_tex: Which of the following is false about the rational function defined by $f(x)=\dfrac{x-2}{x^{2}-2x-3}$?

options.A: Its graph never crosses the x-axis.
options.B: The lines x = −1 and x = 3 are vertical asymptotes of its graph.
options.C: The line y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote of its graph.

explanation_steps: A: f(2) = 0, so the graph crosses the x-axis at (2, 0) – FALSE.
B: the denominator is 0 at x = 3 and x = −1 and the numerator is not – true.
C: degree of numerator (1) < degree of denominator (2) ⇒ y = 0 is the horizontal asymptote – true.
tips: x-intercepts come from zeros of the numerator (that are not zeros of the denominator).

options.A: The graph crosses the x-axis at x = −1
options.B: x = 2 and x = −2 are vertical asymptotes

explanation_steps: deg numerator < deg denominator ⇒ horizontal asymptote y = 0, not y = 1.
f(−1) = 0 ✓, denominator zero at ±2 ✓, f(0) = 1/(−4) ✓. Answer: C.

questions.stem: In a triangle ABC, AB = c units, AC = b units and BC = a units, then the value of cos(∠ABC) is equal to
explanation_steps: ∠ABC is at vertex B; the side opposite B is AC = b, and the sides forming the angle are a (BC) and c (AB).
Law of cosines: b² = a² + c² − 2ac·cos B ⇒ cos B = (a² + c² − b²)/(2ac). Answer: A.

questions.stem: Suppose a student measures opposite angles of two intersecting lines and found out that the two measurements are equal. Then which of the following is a correct deduction based on the single observation of the student?

options.A: A theorem can be deduced "Opposite angles of intersecting lines are congruent".
options.B: It can be taken as a proof for "Opposite angles of intersecting lines are congruent".
options.C: It can be a basis for a conjecture "Opposite angles of intersecting lines are congruent".
options.D: It can be a basis to formulate an axiom "Opposite angles of intersecting lines are congruent".

explanation_steps: A single measurement (inductive observation) cannot prove a general statement, so it is neither a proof nor a theorem (A, B false).
An axiom is accepted without proof as a starting point of the system, not formed from one measurement (D false).
An observation that suggests a general statement not yet proved gives a CONJECTURE. Answer: C.
tips: Conjecture = an educated guess based on observations; theorem = a statement proved from axioms, definitions and earlier theorems.

explanation_steps: Axioms (postulates) are the unproved starting statements; theorems are proved from them.

questions.stem:
Given a circle with center O. If the measure of minor arc AB = 100° and the measure of minor arc CD = 110°, then the measure of ∠AXD is equal to
(Figure: chords AC and BD of the circle intersect at X; AC passes through the centre O; chord BC is also drawn.)
questions.image_alt: Circle with centre O. Points A (upper left), B (left), D (right) and C (lower right) on the circle. Chord AC passes through O (a diameter). Chord BD crosses AC at X near D. Chord BC and chord AB are also drawn.
explanation_steps: X is the intersection of chords AC and BD. The angle formed by two chords intersecting inside a circle is half the sum of the intercepted arcs.
∠AXB (and its vertical angle ∠CXD) intercept arcs AB and CD: ∠AXB = ½(100° + 110°) = 105°.
∠AXD is supplementary to ∠AXB: ∠AXD = 180° − 105° = 75°. (Using the diameter AC: arc BC = 180° − 100° = 80°, arc AD = 180° − 110° = 70°, ∠AXD = ½(70° + 80°) = 75° – the same.)
75° is not among the options. The item is defective; A (85°) is only the nearest value and is keyed provisionally. Low confidence.
tips: Chords intersecting inside: angle = ½(sum of the intercepted arcs). Secants meeting outside: angle = ½(difference of the arcs).

In a circle with center R, CD is tangent to the circle at point B. Point A is on the circle and RE ⟂ AB as shown in the figure below. If AB = 6√3 cm and RE = 6 cm, then m(∠ABC) is equal to
(Figure: RE is a radius drawn perpendicular to chord AB, meeting the circle at E; the tangent line passes through B with C above and D below.)
questions.image_alt: Circle with centre R. Horizontal chord AB (A left, B right). A vertical segment from R down through the chord meets the circle at E, perpendicular to AB. A tangent line touches the circle at B, running from C (upper right) to D (lower left).
explanation_steps: In the figure E is on the circle, so RE = 6 cm is a radius: r = 6.
RE ⟂ AB bisects the chord: half-chord = 3√3. With r = 6: sin(½∠ARB) = 3√3/6 = √3/2 ⇒ ½∠ARB = 60° ⇒ central angle ∠ARB = 120°, so the minor arc AB (through E) = 120°.
Tangent–chord angle = ½ of the intercepted arc: ∠ABD (towards D, intercepting the minor arc AEB) = 60°.
∠ABC is its supplement (intercepts the major arc 240°): ∠ABC = 180° − 60° = 120°. Answer: D.
tips: Angle between a tangent and a chord = half the arc it cuts off.

questions.stem_tex: B1. Solve the following equation and inequality. a) $2x-7=8-3x$ (2 points) b) Solve $\dfrac{(x-1)(x+2)}{(x+3)(x-4)}<0$ (3 points)
explanation_steps: b) Critical numbers: zeros of the numerator x = 1, x = −2; zeros of the denominator x = −3, x = 4 (always excluded).
Sign chart on the intervals (−∞, −3), (−3, −2), (−2, 1), (1, 4), (4, ∞): the expression is +, −, +, −, + (each factor changes sign at its own zero).
The expression is negative on (−3, −2) and (1, 4). Endpoints are excluded (strict inequality; −3 and 4 make the denominator zero).
marking_points: b) critical numbers −3, −2, 1, 4 identified (1); correct sign chart / test values (1); solution (−3, −2) ∪ (1, 4) with open endpoints (1)
tips: Put ALL four critical numbers on the number line; test one value in each interval (e.g. x = 0: (−1)(2)/((3)(−4)) = 1/6 > 0).
Never multiply both sides of a rational inequality by an expression whose sign is unknown.

questions.stem: B2. Given the polynomials x⁵ − x⁴ + x³ + x² − 1 and x² − 2x + 1, then using the long method of division of polynomials, divide x⁵ − x⁴ + x³ + x² − 1 by x² − 2x + 1 and find the quotient and the remainder. (3 points)
questions.answer: Quotient Q(x) = x³ + x² + 2x + 4; remainder R(x) = 6x − 5. So x⁵ − x⁴ + x³ + x² − 1 = (x² − 2x + 1)(x³ + x² + 2x + 4) + (6x − 5).
explanation_steps: Write the dividend with all powers: x⁵ − x⁴ + x³ + x² + 0x − 1.
x⁵ ÷ x² = x³; x³(x² − 2x + 1) = x⁵ − 2x⁴ + x³; subtract → x⁴ + 0x³ + x².
x⁴ ÷ x² = x²; x²(x² − 2x + 1) = x⁴ − 2x³ + x²; subtract → 2x³ + 0x² + 0x.
Check: (x² − 2x + 1)(x³ + x² + 2x + 4) + 6x − 5 = x⁵ − x⁴ + x³ + x² − 1 ✓ (verified with sympy).
marking_points: First two quotient terms x³ + x² with correct subtractions (1)
tips: Insert 0 for missing powers (here 0x) so the columns line up.
Stop when the degree of the remainder is less than the degree of the divisor.

questions.stem:
B3. The square DEFG is inscribed in the right angled triangle ABC, where C is the right angle, as shown in the figure (D and E on AB, G on AC, F on BC). Then prove the following:
a) △ADG ~ △GCF (1 point)
b) △ADG ~ △FEB (1 point)
c) (DE)² = AD × EB (1 point)
questions.image_alt: Right triangle ABC with the right angle at C at the top and hypotenuse AB horizontal at the bottom. Square DEFG stands on AB: D and E on AB, G on side AC and F on side BC.
questions.answer: a) ∠ADG = 90° = ∠GCF and ∠AGD = ∠GFC (corresponding angles, GF ∥ AB), so △ADG ~ △GCF (AA). b) ∠ADG = 90° = ∠FEB and ∠DAG = ∠EFB (both equal 90° − ∠B, since ∠A + ∠B = 90°), so △ADG ~ △FEB (AA). c) From b): AD/FE = DG/EB ⇒ AD × EB = DG × FE = DE × DE = (DE)², because DG = FE = DE (sides of the square).

subparts.label: a
subparts.question: Prove △ADG ~ △GCF
steps: GF ∥ AB gives equal corresponding angles

explanation_steps: The symbol ≃ in the paper stands for 'is similar to' (~): the triangles have different sizes, so they cannot be congruent.
Facts about the square: DE = EF = FG = GD, all angles 90°, GF ∥ AB, GD ⟂ AB and FE ⟂ AB.

a) ∠ADG = 90° (GD ⟂ AB) and ∠GCF = 90° (given). GF ∥ AB with transversal AC gives ∠CGF = ∠CAB; in △ADG, ∠AGD = 90° − ∠A and in △GCF, ∠GFC = 90° − ∠CGF = 90° − ∠A. So two pairs of angles are equal ⇒ △ADG ~ △GCF (AA). [Correspondence A↔G, D↔C, G↔F.]
b) ∠ADG = ∠FEB = 90°. In right △ABC, ∠A + ∠B = 90°; in right △FEB, ∠EFB = 90° − ∠B = ∠A = ∠DAG. ⇒ △ADG ~ △FEB (AA). [A↔F, D↔E, G↔B.]
c) Corresponding sides are proportional: AD/FE = DG/EB. Cross-multiply: AD·EB = DG·FE. Since DG = FE = DE, (DE)² = AD × EB.
marking_points: a) two pairs of equal angles with reasons, AA (1)
b) two pairs of equal angles with reasons, AA (1)
c) correct proportion from b) and substitution DG = FE = DE (1)
tips: Similarity proofs: name the equal angles with reasons (right angles, parallel lines, complementary angles) and state AA.
Write the correspondence in the right order before writing the ratio of sides.

questions.stem:
B4. Given the function f(x) = 2ˣ⁺¹ − 4.
a) Find its domain and range (1 point)
b) Find its intercepts and asymptote if there are any (1 point)
c) Sketch the graph (2 points)
questions.answer: a) Domain: all real numbers ℝ; range: {y | y > −4} = (−4, ∞). b) y-intercept (0, −2); x-intercept (1, 0); horizontal asymptote y = −4 (no vertical asymptote). c) Increasing exponential curve: the graph of y = 2ˣ shifted 1 unit left and 4 units down; passes through (−1, −3), (0, −2), (1, 0), (2, 4); approaches y = −4 as x → −∞.

subparts.label: c
subparts.question: Sketch
subparts.answer: Increasing curve through (−1, −3), (0, −2), (1, 0), (2, 4), approaching y = −4 on the left

explanation_steps: a) 2ˣ⁺¹ is defined for every real x ⇒ domain ℝ. Since 2ˣ⁺¹ > 0, f(x) > −4, and every value above −4 is reached ⇒ range (−4, ∞).
b) y-intercept: f(0) = 2 − 4 = −2. x-intercept: 2ˣ⁺¹ = 4 = 2² ⇒ x + 1 = 2 ⇒ x = 1. As x → −∞, 2ˣ⁺¹ → 0, so y = −4 is a horizontal asymptote.
c) Table of values: x = −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 gives y = −3.75, −3.5, −3, −2, 0, 4. Draw the dashed asymptote y = −4, plot the points and join them with a smooth increasing curve.
marking_points: a) domain ℝ and range y > −4 (1)
b) both intercepts and the asymptote y = −4 (1)
c) asymptote drawn (½), correct intercepts plotted (½), correct increasing shape approaching the asymptote (1)
tips: f(x) = 2ˣ⁺¹ − 4 is y = 2ˣ translated 1 unit left and 4 units down – the asymptote moves from y = 0 to y = −4.
